crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Drafting Proposals from Past Work
children.blurb: Drafting proposals from past work covers the reuse of prior aims, methods, preliminary results, budgets, and biosketches in a new grant submission.

children.name: Funder Formatting and Compliance
children.blurb: Funder formatting and compliance covers the rules a funding body sets for how a proposal must look, what it must contain, and how it must be submitted.

children.name: Budgets and Allowable Costs
children.blurb: Budgets and allowable costs in AI research grants cover the direct and indirect expenses that a sponsor will reimburse, from personnel salaries and fringe benefits to equipment, travel, materials, publication fees, and the compute and data storage that AI projects often require.

children.name: Finding Collaborators
children.blurb: Finding collaborators for grant proposals is the work of identifying people, groups, and institutions whose expertise, resources, or access complements a proposed project.

children.name: Predicting Proposal Success
children.blurb: Predicting proposal success is the use of data and models to estimate whether a grant application will be funded, often before or during review.

sections.body: Grant proposals and funding form the part of AI research where tools help write, check, budget, assemble teams, and target research bids. In practice, AI systems draft sections from a researcher's past papers and prior proposals, suggest aims and impact statements, and rewrite text to match a funder's tone. They also scan calls for eligibility rules, page limits, and required sections, then flag missing items before submission. Budget tools map costs to agency categories and check whether each line is allowable under a program's rules. Collaborator tools search publication records, coauthorship networks, and institutional profiles to suggest partners with complementary skills. Success prediction tools estimate how a proposal might score by comparing it with funded abstracts and review criteria.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts of this work are now routine. Formatting checks, reference validation, and first pass drafting are reliable when the funder's rules are clear and the source material is well organized. Budget assistance can catch common errors, but it cannot know every institution's internal rates or a program officer's unwritten preferences. Finding collaborators is useful for discovery, yet it does not replace a conversation about roles, credit, and workload. Predicting proposal success remains the weakest area, because review outcomes depend on panel composition, current priorities, and arguments that are hard to score from text alone, and the site's 135 research papers are a library of research works, not a database of funded proposals. AI can also invent citations, misread a solicitation, or leak confidential ideas if used carelessly, so human review stays central.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages in this section follow the life of a proposal from idea to submission. Drafting Proposals from Past Work shows how to turn earlier papers and reports into new text without copying yourself. Funder Formatting and Compliance covers the rules that decide whether a proposal is even reviewed, including templates, limits, and required attachments. Budgets and Allowable Costs explains how to build a cost plan that matches agency categories and survives an audit. Finding Collaborators looks at how AI can suggest partners from publication and project records, and Predicting Proposal Success examines what models can and cannot say about review outcomes. Read them together as a chain, because a strong draft can still fail on a missed compliance item, an unallowable cost, or a weak team.
